name: Simulation
subtitle: Generate observable world behavior via system rules; the core is variables, causal chains, and explainability.
demoRuleHint: Example rule: Set resource generation rate → Observe population growth → Adjust resource allocation.
problemsSolved: Make causal chains observable and explainable, avoiding 'black-box number crunching'.
Provide steady states and boundary conditions to prevent system runaway or boring stagnation.
Give players clear intervention levers (parameters/strategies/resources) so adjustments are effective.
learningGoals: Beginner: understand the simulation loop — set variables → system evolves → observe metrics → adjust — and reproduce one parameter intervention in the demo
Intermediate: write the variable and causal-chain contract (update rules, propagation delays, boundary conditions), and tune the feedback-period length
Advanced: design steady states and collapse boundaries (explainable emergence), and verify system vitality with metric variance, collapse rate, and intervention effectiveness
minimalRules: Observation: Let players see key metric changes.
systemLoopHint: Input (parameters/strategies) → Evolution (rule updates) → Observation (metric changes) → Decision (success/failure) → Adjustment → New input

combos.effect: Drive system evolution and expansion with long-term goals.
Alter system trajectory through key decisions.
More realistic world rules bring emergent gameplay.

advancedWarnings: Too many variables reduce explainability; too few variables reduce depth.
Long feedback cycles cause players to lose immediate feedback; short cycles cause excessive system noise.
Overly restricting parameters can spur players to find micro-tuning points, producing richer emergent behavior—limits force exploration of edge states.
advancedAlgoRefs: Evolution: tick updates, event queue, stability control.

demoLab.title: Tax Lever Experiment
demoLab.action: Drag the "Tax Rate" slider from 0.2 to 0.5, "Advance 1 Step" 10 days, and watch money and happiness diverge
demoLab.observe: The tax rate is the start of the causal chain: money surges while happiness slides, and low happiness in turn suppresses pop growth. One lever moves several metrics — the depth of simulation play comes from the propagation delay between variables

demoLab.title: Steady-State Hunt
demoLab.action: Use "Raise Tax (primary)" / "Cut Tax (secondary)" to fine-tune, hunting for the tax band where happiness and money both rise
demoLab.observe: The system reaches a steady state at middle tax rates — both extremes collapse (0% starves the treasury, 60% drives people away). An observable steady-state boundary makes "adjustment works": players find their own optimum instead of memorizing a guide

demoLab.title: Collapse Watch
demoLab.action: Push the tax rate to 0.6 and "Advance 1 Step" for 20 straight days
demoLab.observe: happiness collapses → pop drains → tax revenue actually falls — a Laffer-curve counterintuitive: maximum rate ≠ maximum revenue. Emergent collapse is the core teaching moment of simulation play: when causal chains are observable, collapse becomes explainable

intro.what: Set the rule parameters and watch a little world run itself — management sims, city builders, and The Sims are built on this.
intro.feel: You nudge the tax rate; the next day money is up but the people are unhappy; nudge it again and the population starts draining — every knob pulls the whole web, and watching the system react is more addictive than direct control.
intro.why: A training ground for "systems thinking" — causal chains, emergence, and steady states, all mystical-sounding concepts you can actually touch here.

concept: Simulation play lets the rules tell the story themselves: players do not operate outcomes directly — they adjust variables and watch causal chains propagate into emergent behavior. The hard part is not the variable count — it is explainability and steady states: too many variables and causality becomes unreadable, too few and the system lacks depth, and both runaway collapse and stagnant boredom are simulation failures. Players say "this system is fascinating" because every adjustment can be explained by its causal chain.
designNotes: Propagation delay is the source of depth: a tax change hits money instantly, happiness slowly, and population last — the time lag of one lever moving several metrics is what gives a system its "feel."

Extreme parameters must collapse: zero tax starves the treasury, full tax drives everyone away — a system that dies at both ends has a middle steady state worth hunting; if every setting is "fine," the simulation has nothing to explore.
Constraints spark emergence (counterintuitive): with parameters fenced in, players actively explore edge states hunting for fine-tuning points — give them boundless freedom and they get bored fast.
